Maladaptive Strategies.value: Seeing people that I socialised with before the event

Threat.value: My body reacts to danger before I have even had time to think
I study people's faces and body language to detect if they are a threat
I have difficulty falling asleep because I need to stay alert

Memory.value: Sometimes I can recall what happened but feel completely numb, as if it happened to a stranger
When the memory comes back it feels completely real across all my senses at once
When memories come to mind of what happened, I feel my body is in the same position as when the frightening event occurred.

Negative Appraisals.value: I have lost my connection to my community and culture
I feel dirty or contaminated because of what happened
People are not what they seem

issues.item: Triggers: Visual (Water/Flooding): Water, flooding, or large bodies of water
issues.explanation: For police violence, water/flooding and soil/outdoor smells are hard to reconcile as primary trauma-linked triggers when the rest of the profile contains no content suggesting a water, outdoor, or environmental trauma context. Bus riding could fit policing/public surveillance, but these other triggers point toward a different trauma setting.

issues.item: Triggers: Olfactory (Earth/Outdoor): Soil or outdoor smells
issues.explanation: The appraisal of lost connection to community/culture is possible after police violence, but in this profile it is not supported by the selected triggers or memories, which center on acute sensory reliving and bodily threat rather than social exclusion, community rupture, or cultural shame. It feels disconnected from the rest of the formulation.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Lost Community: I have lost my connection to my community and culture
issues.explanation: Within the Memory node, emotionless recall can coexist with reliving, but combining complete numb detachment with full multisensory reliving and bodily reenactment as parallel core memory experiences is somewhat tensioned. More importantly, the reliving items imply a very specific embodied trauma scene, yet the trigger set does not reflect cues plausibly tied to that scene.

issues.item: Memory: Full Sensory Reliving: When the memory comes back it feels completely real across all my senses at once
issues.explanation: Mirror checking is difficult to explain from the rest of the profile. The threat items concern rapid bodily danger detection, reading faces, and sleep vigilance; the memories concern reliving; and the appraisals concern distrust/contamination/community loss. Mirror checking suggests appearance/body checking or checking for signs on oneself, but no associated appraisal or memory content supports it. It does not cohere well with the police violence formulation here.

vignette: Asha, a 25-year-old South Asian woman working as a counselor, has been struggling since she experienced police violence during an event in her community. The traumatic experience left her with a deep sense of loss and contamination, as if the violence had seeped into her very being. On the day of the incident, Asha was riding the bus to work when she noticed the tension on board. Suddenly, several officers entered the vehicle, their faces stern and imposing. As they approached, she felt an overwhelming surge of fear. Her body reacted instantly-her heart racing, palms sweating-as if her instincts were warning her before her mind could process what was happening. Since that day, Asha has found herself avoiding public transport altogether. The memory of the bus ride triggers a flood of sensations and emotions. When she does encounter reminders, such as the smell of soil or outdoor scents, she feels acutely aware of any authority figures nearby. This constant vigilance is draining; she studies every face and body language, looking for signs of potential danger. Her difficulty falling asleep further exacerbates her stress, as she remains alert to ensure no threat can catch her off guard. Asha's memories are both vivid and numbing. Sometimes, the event plays out in full sensory detail, feeling completely real; other times, it feels detached, as if something happened to someone else entirely. During these episodes, she often finds herself reliving not just the memory but also the physical sensations of that day-her body positioning itself instinctively as if reenacting the scene. This cycle has left Asha feeling isolated and disconnected from her community. She had come to believe that people are not what they seem, and this distrust extends even to those who have always been supportive. The contamination she feels deepens her sense of estrangement. Her social contacts have dwindled, as she avoids seeing friends or colleagues for fear of triggering these memories and responses. To cope with the overwhelming sense of threat, Asha often hides her face with her hands, checking mirrors frequently to ensure no one is watching her. These behaviors stem from a deep-seated belief that people are inherently untrustworthy, leading her to withdraw further into herself. This withdrawal only reinforces her negative appraisals and makes everyday activities increasingly stressful. The weight of these experiences has taken a significant toll on Asha's work as a counselor. She finds it challenging to engage fully with clients due to the constant fear that someone might betray her or pose a threat. Her daily environment is fraught with potential triggers, making each day an exercise in managing her reactions and trying to maintain some semblance of normalcy. What frightens Asha most is the relentless cycle of fear and distrust. She had hoped for a way back to feeling connected to her community and living without constant vigilance, but these hopes have been increasingly overshadowed by the pervasive sense of danger and contamination. Finally seeking help, she is determined to break free from this cycle, hoping to regain trust in herself and others. The combination of triggers, maladaptive strategies, negative appraisals, memory issues, and heightened threat perception has created a complex web that tightens around Asha's daily life. She now recognizes the urgent need for intervention to reclaim her sense of self and connection with the world.
